title: REST, JSON and HTTP methods
basic: An API request has a method, URL, headers and sometimes a body. JSON is a data format; REST is an architectural style, not a synonym for every JSON endpoint.
intermediate: GET reads resources; POST often creates or invokes an operation; PATCH applies a partial update. Interpret status, content type and response body together.
advanced: Document the contract, permitted methods, required fields and error shape. A syntactically valid request can still violate ownership or business rules.
tools: curl displays a single exchange; jq selects JSON fields; Postman organizes repeatable requests. Compare one valid request with one invalid request.
practice: Start the supplied fixed-mode app, then request /api/profile without a credential: expect 401. A 200 HTML login page would not prove authenticated access.

title: API keys, bearer tokens, JWT and OAuth
basic: An API key may identify an application rather than a human. A bearer token grants whatever authority the service associates with it. JWT is a token format; OAuth is a delegation framework.
intermediate: Check whether tokens are intended for this API and whether expiry, issuer, audience and signature are validated. Decoding claims does not validate a JWT.
advanced: Separate access tokens, refresh tokens and identity tokens. Model scope, revocation and client type. An authenticated request still needs object and function authorization.
tools: Use Postman local variables for the fixture token; Burp Repeater compares authenticated and unauthenticated responses. Never paste real credentials into public token-decoding websites.
practice: The casebook uses opaque in-memory tokens and synthetic MFA, not JWT or OAuth. Login gives a pending token; /mfa produces a full token in fixed mode.

title: BOLA / IDOR: object ownership
basic: Broken Object-Level Authorization allows a caller to access an object outside their permitted scope. Guessable identifiers alone do not establish the weakness.
intermediate: Use Alice and Bob with known objects. Compare Alice own invoice, Alice requesting Bob invoice, and Bob own invoice. Change one variable at a time.
advanced: Enforce tenant and owner rules at the service or data-access boundary. Unpredictable identifiers cannot replace permission checks. Include lists and nested resources.
tools: Use Burp Repeater tabs labelled Alice-own, Alice-other and Bob-own. The supplied Postman collection exercises the same fixed-mode matrix.
practice: In fixed mode Alice gets invoice 1 with 200, invoice 2 with 403; Bob gets invoice 2 with 200. Vulnerable mode deliberately permits Alice to read invoice 2.

title: Broken function-level authorization
basic: Function authorization decides whether a role may perform an operation, such as issuing refunds or changing permissions. It differs from which object a caller may read.
intermediate: Build a role-by-operation matrix including anonymous, ordinary and administrator accounts. Check the server endpoint even when its UI button is hidden.
advanced: Apply policy consistently across versions and alternate methods. An admin-looking URL does not prove a function is privileged; use the documented policy and observed action.
tools: Use Postman folders for roles and Burp Repeater for one authorized fixture operation at a time. ZAP passive review can flag response observations, but cannot infer the business role policy.
practice: The included fixture has no administrator-only refund route. Use a design worksheet for this topic; do not claim its role-field test proves complete function authorization.
code:
Role | Operation | Expected | Observed
Anonymous | read invoice | deny | record
Owner | read own invoice | allow | record
User | administrator operation in a separate lab | deny | record

title: Data exposure and mass assignment
basic: Read-side exposure returns fields a caller should not receive. Mass assignment accepts fields the caller must not control.
intermediate: Use explicit output schemas and writable-field allowlists. Test a permitted display_name update separately from an attempted role update.
advanced: Inspect nested fields, bulk updates and serialization paths. Browser-side hiding does not remove a field from the response or enforce a write restriction.
tools: Use jq or Postman to inspect response fields and Burp Repeater to compare two small JSON bodies. Do not treat every returned field as sensitive without context.
practice: Fixed mode rejects PATCH /api/profile with role using 400, preserves role=user, and accepts display_name. Vulnerable mode intentionally accepts the role field.

title: Rate limits and resource consumption
basic: Request rate, response size and computational cost are different limits. A single costly operation may consume more resources than many simple ones.
intermediate: Test a small documented boundary in an isolated lab. Record pagination, body-size and timeout rules; stop when the agreed limit or stop condition is reached.
advanced: A rate limiter needs a chosen identity and window. Consider shared users, expensive operations and recovery. Do not infer adequate limits from one 429 response.
tools: Use one curl request for a pagination boundary and unit tests with controlled time for rate-limit logic. Avoid load tools on this teaching server.
practice: The fixture allows list limits 1 through 10 and rejects 11. This proves input-bound validation only: it has no rate limiter and is not a load-testing target.
code:
GET /api/invoices?limit=1  -> expected 200 with a full token
GET /api/invoices?limit=11 -> expected 400 with a full token

title: GraphQL security fundamentals
basic: GraphQL defines typed operations and selected response fields. Queries, mutations and subscriptions need appropriate authorization.
intermediate: Review object and field permissions, pagination and error content. An HTTP 200 can still contain an errors array; inspect the response body.
advanced: Use depth, breadth and cost controls appropriate to the schema. Disabling introspection does not establish authorization or prevent expensive operations.
tools: Use GraphiQL or Postman with a separately configured local GraphQL server and its known schema. Check one allowed object and one denied object.
practice: The provided REST fixture has no GraphQL endpoint. The query below is a schema-dependent reading example, not a command for port 8901.

title: Remediation, regression tests and reporting
basic: Reproduce the smallest policy failure with synthetic data, repair the authorization or validation rule, then rerun the same test.
intermediate: Retest a legitimate operation as well as the denied case. Keep separate expectations for vulnerable and fixed teaching modes.
advanced: A green test establishes only its asserted properties. Note untested protocols, roles, token formats, concurrency and infrastructure controls.
tools: Use Python unittest for deterministic regressions, Postman for readable request sequences and Burp for manual comparisons. Link each finding to evidence and its repair.
practice: Download the lab ZIP, start the casebook in vulnerable mode, run the API exercise, stop it, then restart fixed mode and repeat. A passing vulnerable-mode exercise confirms the intentional weakness.
code:
python3 -m unittest -v test_lab
python3 exercise.py --expect fixed --case api
